What about LLMs?

Educators at all levels and in all disciplines are experimenting to try to figure out the
long-term implications of large language models like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, etc.
In computer science, we're also thinking about code generation tools like Cursor,
Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Windsurf, etc.

This term, let's look for and talk with each other about opportunities to use the LLMs to help
us learn and do our work effectively. I want you learning, and if LLMs can help that to happen,
I want us to collaborate to figure out how and share our ideas.

For this class, you may use LLMs as you see fit, but if you use LLMs to
generate anything you submit as homework, I want you to tell me about it.
If any of your submitted work includes any LLM output
(verbatim or paraphrased), I require you to include a file called

LLM.txt
(or
LLM-name-of-assignment.txt
)
(or .md, .docx, .pdf,...) with your submission.
Your
LLM.*
file should consist of a sequence of sections, each of which describes
a portion of your submission that came from LLM output. Each such section should include:

What subset of your homework submission are we talking about?

Which LLM did you use to generate that subset?

What exact prompt(s) did you use to generate the output?

Anything else you want to say.

In the previous section, I said "to get points for an assignment, you need to write most
of the code yourself". This statement also applies if you're getting help from
an LLM.

One more thing: I'd love to see you share your stories of AI successes, failures,
or madcap adventures. I have created a channel named #ai in our Slack workspace for
this purpose.

Questions about this policy or specific situations?—bring it up in #questions on Slack,
raise it in class, or talk to me in office hours.

We require that you disable AI extensions from your programming
environment and in general that you do not use AI tools. These
tools may give a quick answer but they undermine learning and
retention.
You may not use AI tools for practice problems.

Generative AI

You may not use AI tools for any part of work that you will submit
for credit.

This includes but is
not limited to generating solutions, checking solutions, explaining
tasks or solutions, formatting code, adding comments to code,
or
generating test cases.

Use of these tools on assignments will be reported as an academic
integrity violation.

Your goal in this course is to learn and acquire skills. This is
achieved through hands-on practice, which takes time and can feel
frustrating.

Using generative AI or other improper help for this practice
negates learning and mastering new skills.

To best support your own learning, you should complete all graded
assignments in this course yourself, without any use of generative
artificial intelligence (AI) to create your solutions. Please refrain
from using AI tools to generate any content (text, video, audio, images,
code, etc.) for an assignment. Passing off any AI generated content as
your own (e.g., cutting and pasting, or paraphrasing AI content) constitutes
a violation of CMU’s academic integrity policy. If you have any questions
about using generative AI in this course please email or talk to course staff.

This course content is not only interesting but also extremely valuable, esepcially for job interviews. Any usage of AI tools is truly only doing yourself a long-term disservice. You must
not make use of AI tools, LLM tools, or any other software or service that generates code, proofs, written explanations, or any other content that could be the subject of a homework problem
. This includes all LLM tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and any similar tools or derrivative tools based on them or that uses them. Similarly, AI-editing and code completion tools such as GitHub CoPilot must be turned off and avoided. Please be aware that code generated by these tools is
often incorrect
, and even when not,
it is easy to distinguish from student-written code and thus very easy for us to detect
. You will be caught if you submit homework that contains code generated by AI tools.

All work that you present must be your own. Thus, generative AI
tools may not be used to generate any part of your assignment
submission. (Yes, these tools are awesome, but we've designed
this course to minimize the amount of code/material that you need to
write, so you should be able to complete the assignments in a timely
manner without these aids.)

AI Tools are a valuable tool for supporting both novices and experts.
However, their usage can easily lead students into
violating the above rules, especially as those tools may be trained using
sources that would be disallowed to directly be used. If you do use an
AI Tool, you should confine your interaction along the same rules as other
external sources, such as only having high-level discussions and making
sure to cite and document your usage.

In brief, students should avoid any copy-paste interactions with AI Tools,
and cite what they do.

You
may not
upload the code you write for a lab assignment
(or even parts of it) to any AI tool (cloud-based or locally hosted or
in your IDE) nor give the AI tool access to the code (or even parts of
it). Much like asking a friend for help and providing access to your
code, the help you get is most likely going to be an AIV, so it is not
permitted. Examples of AI Tools include ChatGPT, github copilot,
Gemini, Claude, and many others.

MOST IMPORTANTLY, DON'T USE ChatGPT. It does weird things which are
pretty easy for me to catch , and it was a very big pet peeve of mine last semester. If
you use it, I'll assume you are completely disrespecting me.
If you are caught using unauthorized resources, I will award you a -100% on the assignment for
the first offense and a -200% on the second, doubling each time. Note this does not mean a 100%
turns into 0%; you will receive a -100%. Anyone that knowingly assists someone in using
unauthorized resources or cheating will also earn a -100% on the assignment.
Also, note that the value of the programs has been reduced so that even if students use ChatGPT,
it won't significantly affect a student's grade positively. In fact, it's likely to reduce their
understanding of the material, hence lowering their quiz grades.

In
short, no AI and no getting "signficant" help from someone other than the course
instructor or teaching assistant.)

This is a new item I am adding to the course syllabus due to AI. When I ask questions live, I can
quickly tell the "level " of a student's understanding. (With the advent of AI, code that stude nts
submit unfortunately isn't always an accurate signal of their actual understanding.)

Your group is allowed to and encouraged to use AI for this project if you deem that
it would be helpful.
you may not use any electronic devices (laptops, phones, AI Glasses, tablets, e-readers, etc.)

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools including but not limited to Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, etc. can be useful for student programmers and professional programmers alike. However, they can also hinder the learning process. Outside of class assignments and exams, I leave it up to you to decide how to use these tools. For example, AI tools might prove useful for creating examples of programs that you can learn from. If you want to see a quick example of a C++ program that defines and uses a function, for example, AI tools may be able to give this to you, and it may be quicker to ask an AI tool than to skim through the textbook. The constant temptation will be to use AI tools to write code for your assignments and exams. I expect you to refrain from using AI tools in this way.
You are not allowed to use AI for any coursework, including both assignments and exams.

Any student who submits code obtained using an AI application must cite
both the AI app and the specification submitted to the AI to generate the code. Failure to
cite either the AI app or the specs used will receive a zero for the assignment.

You may not turn in any AI-generated code or written text. This includes the output of AI code assistants. Copying text or code from generative AI software either by hand or electronically is academic dishonesty. If I see you using software like Co-Pilot it is considered academic dishonesty.

In general, the use of generative AI (like ChatGPT) in CS 151 is discouraged. You must include an AI usage statement in each project report. If you use a generative AI tool like ChatGPT to assist with your projects or reports, you should acknowledge which part you used it on and include the prompts that you used. Not doing so breaches academic integrity policies. It's your responsibility to verify the correctness of the answers from generative AI. You will not lose points for claiming to use generative AI but you will lose points for incorrect answers.

Your AI Usage Statement must include:

Statement on if you used AI on this project.

A reflection on how you used AI for the project including software used. If you did not use AI for this project, complete the AI reflection question.

Include all prompts that you used and how you incorporated them into your project or report.

You cannot receive extension points without an AI usage statement.

Labs have the same AI policy as your lecture section.

Understanding and using AI are important skills that you will master as part of your CS education at Colby, and the following policy will provide a controlled way for you to use AI to your learning advantage in this course:

Students may use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) solely for understanding concepts, reviewing examples, or receiving feedback on their code. These tools can be valuable for clarifying ideas and enhancing comprehension.

Using AI to generate any code, solutions, or answers is strictly prohibited and considered academic misconduct. All submitted work must be entirely the student’s own effort.

Students must be able to demonstrate their understanding of solutions through verbal explanations, either in class discussions, office hours, or during assessments.

When AI tools are used for understanding concepts, reviewing examples, or receiving feedback related to a specific assignment or project, students must:

Clearly indicate the extent and nature of the AI’s contribution.

Be prepared to discuss and explain the submitted work during office hours or in class

The use of AI code completion tools, such as GitHub Copilot or other similar platforms, is completely prohibited. Students must write and develop their code independently to ensure they are practicing and reinforcing the skills taught in the course.

Here are some examples of prompts that do not violate the AI policy:

“What is the difference between a stack and a queue?”

“How does a binary search tree work?”

“I'm encountering this error message 'IndexError: list index out of range' when running my code. What does it mean, and how can I fix it?”

“Can you explain how Dijkstra's algorithm works? I'm trying to understand its steps and how it’s applied in practice.”

“Can you help me debug my code? Don't generate any code, just help me understand why my code is not working.”

Here are some examples of prompts that violate the AI policy:

“Can you provide me with a solution to this problem?”

“Can you write a function that ...?”

“Can you generate a code snippet that ....?”

“Can you fix my code so that ...?”

Violations of this policy, including the use of AI for generating code or failure to properly document AI interactions, may result in penalties ranging from a warning to a failing grade for the assignment or course, in accordance with the institution's academic integrity policy.

Effective use of AI has become a core skill in modern computer science and related fields. I encourage you to use AI in this course to build your proficiency. However, with freedom comes responsibility: use AI to enhance your learning, not replace it. You must find balance in your usage so that you learn effectively — this looks different for everyone and requires experimentation.

A primary goal of this course is to prepare you as an AI tool builder. That requires hands-on practice with coding, design, and analysis. If AI does that heavy lifting for you, you have gone too far. Here are a few ideas to guide your AI usage:

Code review:
Write a method yourself, then have AI help you check your work. Make sure you understand any suggestions or fixes the AI proposes. Never accept fixes blindly; your solution may be better aligned with the project goals.

Explore alternative implementations:
Ask AI for more readable or efficient implementations. You might learn about an approach that you did not consider!

Mock quizzes:
Have AI quiz you on concepts, code, or results.

Ultimately, you are responsible for all the code and analyses that you turn in; AI cannot take the blame for shortcomings.
Here are several points to keep in mind:

For base projects, you should only use Python packages listed in
Software
. Do not let AI convince you otherwise.

Be cautious of AI suggestions that involve esoteric or exotic functions or overly complex implementations. If you cannot read and understand them, do not include them!

If you get help from other sources (e.g., instructors, TAs, internet, generative AI etc), you should cite the sources and the nature of help that you got in Section 3 of the justification of correctness document associated with the assignment. Here are some examples of citations:
* “I ran into a bug with function X in my code. I discussed this with person Y and discovered that the source of the bug was Z.”
* “I did not understand concept X. So I conversed with chatbot A to clarify some misconceptions. I verified the insights from this conversation using websites Y (link) and Z (link).”
* “I forgot how the syntax for X worked in Java. I found the solution on website Y (link)

Generative AI systems (like Claude, ChatGPT, etc), if used correctly, can serve as powerful tools for learning and idea refinement. In this course, you can use generative AI systems to learn about concepts iteratively through a conversation (much like you would have a conversation with a peer, TA or an instructor). However, you cannot ask these systems to directly give you answers or write code for you. This is because I believe the intellectual growth you can get from working through a difficult problem and discovering the answer for yourself cannot be replicated by just reading a pre-generated answer — and the skills you learn from this course, such as applying algorithmic reasoning to justify correctness, is more important than ever as AI increasingly lowers the barrier to generating code.

Here are some concrete rules that exemplify this (but are not intended to be comprehensive):

Do NOT:
* Give the model a problem description and ask it to sketch an algorithm for you or write you pseudo code.
* Give the model the homework description and ask it to organize the code for you (e.g., generate the necessary function headers, write the main functions etc).
* Give the model a function description and ask it to generate code for you.
* Given some problem description or code, ask the model to generate test cases for you.
* Use the model to write any aspect of the justification of correctness document.

Using the AI system in ways as described above will count as cheating even if you cite the AI system as a source.

You CAN:
* Ask clarification questions about the fundamentals of programming (e.g., “When should I use a public vs. private method in Java?”)
* Ask for conceptual clarifications (e.g., “What is the difference between average case and best case run times?”)
* Try to work through the logic of something you don’t understand (e.g., “Why is the run time of this algorithm [describe] n^2?”)
* Given a problem description and your proposed algorithm and “talk” through the potential fallacies.

Note, for any of these models having the correct “prompt” is necessary. So you may have varying levels of success using these models to gain conceptual understanding, and in many cases just talking to your instructors/ TA/ peers or even doing straight up googling is likely to yield better results. If you do decide to use these models, it is your responsibility to also fact check the insights that you gain.

Remember: Policies around the use of Generative AI tools, like any other course policies, vary across different courses both within and outside the department.
